patient.name: Harold Weisman
patient.chiefComplaint: Syncopal episode, now weak and lightheaded

history.hpi: Patient was walking to the kitchen when he suddenly felt lightheaded and collapsed to the floor, striking a chair on the way down. Witnessed by his wife, who reports he was unresponsive for approximately 15 seconds before waking on his own. He is now awake but weak, pale, and diaphoretic, with ongoing lightheadedness when attempting to sit up.
pastMedical: Coronary artery disease with prior NSTEMI 4 years ago
history.events: Sudden collapse while walking at home, brief loss of consciousness, wife called 911 immediately

scene.dispatch: 82-year-old male, fall with possible loss of consciousness, residence
scene.location: Single-story home, kitchen, patient found on the floor near a dining chair
scene.bystanders: Wife present, witnessed the collapse, called 911 immediately
visualCues: Patient supine on kitchen floor, pale and diaphoretic
Small abrasion to forehead from contact with chair
Empty coffee cup on the table
Patient appears weak, slow to respond to questions

phases.name: Initial Contact
phases.description: Crew arrives to find an 82-year-old male on the kitchen floor, pale, diaphoretic, and weak following a witnessed syncopal episode. He is alert but slow to respond, with a markedly slow and irregular pulse noted on initial palpation.

clinicalPresentation.airway: Patent, speaking in full sentences slowly
clinicalPresentation.circulation: Radial pulse weak and markedly slow and irregular, skin pale and diaphoretic
clinicalPresentation.motorFunction: Strength intact in all extremities, generalized weakness
otherFindings: Small forehead abrasion, no active bleeding
Reports lightheadedness worsens when sitting upright
Denies chest pain, denies shortness of breath
clinicalPresentation.patientSpeech: "I just felt so dizzy... everything went dark for a second."

transitions.condition: Crew recognizes symptomatic bradycardia with hemodynamic instability from complete heart block, establishes IV access, obtains a 12-lead, and administers atropine per protocol as the first-line therapy while preparing for pacing.

phases.name: Assessed and atropine given
phases.description: Crew establishes IV access, applies oxygen, obtains a 12-lead confirming complete heart block, and administers atropine per protocol. As expected with third-degree block, the patient shows no significant improvement in rate or perfusion.
phases.triggerCondition: After recognizing symptomatic bradycardia with hemodynamic instability (BP 78/48, HR 28), the crew establishes IV access and gives atropine 1 mg IV per protocol while simultaneously preparing pacer pads, anticipating that complete heart block often does not respond to atropine.

clinicalPresentation.circulation: Radial pulse weak, slow, irregular; skin remains pale and diaphoretic
otherFindings: 12-lead confirms complete AV dissociation with a ventricular escape rhythm
No change in rate or perfusion after atropine
Patient remains lightheaded when head of cot is raised
clinicalPresentation.patientSpeech: "That didn't seem to help much, I still feel awful."

expectedActions.shortAction: Apply O2, initiate monitoring, obtain 12-lead EKG, establish IV access
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: Manage airway as necessary. Administer oxygen as appropriate with a target of achieving 94–98% saturation. Initiate monitoring and perform 12-lead EKG. Establish IV access
expectedActions.rationale: Confirms the rhythm as third-degree block and establishes access for medications and pacing.

expectedActions.shortAction: Check blood glucose to rule out hypoglycemia as a contributing cause
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: Check blood glucose and treat hypoglycemia per the Hypoglycemia Guideline and Hyperglycemia Guideline
expectedActions.rationale: Hypoglycemia is a treatable, reversible cause of altered perfusion and must be excluded.

expectedActions.shortAction: Atropine 1 mg IV, may repeat q3-5min (max total 3 mg)
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: Consider the following additional therapies if bradycardia and symptoms or hemodynamic instability continue: Atropine 1 mg IV q 3–5 minutes (maximum total dose of 3 mg)
expectedActions.rationale: First-line pharmacologic therapy per protocol, given while preparing to escalate to pacing.

transitions.condition: Atropine fails to improve rate or perfusion as anticipated with third-degree block; crew proceeds directly to transcutaneous pacing with appropriate sedation/pain control for the paced patient.
Crew initiates transcutaneous pacing but fails to provide sedation or analgesia first, leaving the patient in severe distress from the painful pacing stimulus.

phases.name: TCP initiated with sedation
phases.description: Recognizing atropine's failure in third-degree block, the crew proceeds to transcutaneous pacing with mechanical capture confirmed, along with appropriate sedation/analgesia for patient comfort during pacing.
phases.triggerCondition: After atropine fails to improve the complete heart block, crew moves directly to transcutaneous pacing per protocol, provides ketamine for pain control given the hypotension, and confirms electrical and mechanical capture.

clinicalPresentation.circulation: Palpable radial pulse now synchronous with paced rate, skin warming, less diaphoretic
otherFindings: Transcutaneous pacer capturing at 70 bpm with visible muscle twitch tolerated after sedation
Denies significant pain from pacing after ketamine given
clinicalPresentation.patientSpeech: "That's much more tolerable now, thank you."

expectedActions.shortAction: Ketamine 21 mg IV (85 kg × 0.25 mg/kg = 21.25 mg; max initial 25 mg)
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: Ketamine: 0.25 mg/kg IM, IV or IO (maximum initial dose 25 mg; maximum cumulative dose 100 mg)
expectedActions.rationale: Provides analgesia for the painful pacing stimulus without worsening hypotension, per the protocol's note to consider sedation or pain control with pacing.

expectedActions.shortAction: Initiate transcutaneous pacing at 70 bpm, confirm mechanical capture with palpable pulse
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: Transcutaneous Pacing – If pacing is performed, consider sedation or pain control
expectedActions.rationale: Third-degree block is unlikely to respond to atropine; pacing directly restores an effective rate.

transitions.condition: Pacing capture and sedation are maintained; patient is packaged for transport with continuous reassessment.

phases.name: Capture maintained, prepared for transport
phases.description: The patient remains hemodynamically stable with sustained mechanical capture on the transcutaneous pacer and adequate sedation, transported for further cardiac evaluation.
phases.triggerCondition: With pacing capture confirmed and sedation on board, the patient's perfusion and mentation continue to improve; crew maintains continuous monitoring en route.

clinicalPresentation.circulation: Strong radial pulse synchronous with pacer, skin pink and warm
otherFindings: Sustained electrical and mechanical capture at 70 bpm
Pacer pads and sedation continuously reassessed
clinicalPresentation.patientSpeech: "I feel a lot better, still a little strange with this pacing but tolerable."

expectedActions.shortAction: Continuously reassess capture, sedation level, and vital signs en route
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: Time started or stopped, rate, joules, capture, and response rate
expectedActions.rationale: Pacer capture and sedation depth can change en route and require ongoing monitoring.

phases.name: TCP performed without sedation
phases.description: The crew initiates transcutaneous pacing but skips sedation or pain control. The patient experiences significant distress and pain from the pacing stimulus, becoming agitated and combative, which risks pad displacement and loss of capture.
phases.triggerCondition: Pacing is started without first providing sedation or analgesia, despite the protocol noting that sedation or pain control should be considered with pacing; the patient experiences severe discomfort from the paced muscle contractions.

clinicalPresentation.airway: Patent, crying out with each paced beat
clinicalPresentation.circulation: Palpable pulse synchronous with pacer but patient thrashing
clinicalPresentation.motorFunction: Visible chest wall muscle twitching with each paced impulse, patient attempting to pull away
otherFindings: Patient extremely agitated and combative from pacing discomfort
Pad contact at risk of being disrupted by patient movement
Crew struggling to maintain pad position
clinicalPresentation.patientSpeech: "Stop! It hurts, make it stop, please!"

expectedActions.shortAction: Ketamine 21 mg IV (85 kg × 0.25 mg/kg = 21.25 mg; max initial 25 mg) for pacing discomfort
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: Ketamine: 0.25 mg/kg IM, IV or IO (maximum initial dose 25 mg; maximum cumulative dose 100 mg)
expectedActions.rationale: Rescue analgesia is needed to control severe pacing-related distress and prevent pad displacement or loss of capture.
